b: A communicable chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis .

The World Health Organization (WHO) considers TB the most common cause of death from a single infectious agent , with approximately 1.7 billion infected globally, 8–10 million new cases, and 1.5 million deaths annually.
The reservoir is individuals with active pulmonary disease.
Transmission occurs via inhalation of airborne organisms in aerosols produced during expectoration or from contaminated secretions.
M. tuberculosis are slender rods that are acid-fast (resistant to decolorization with acid-alcohol after staining with carbolfuchsin using the Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorescent auramine-rhodamine stains).
TB is a serious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis . It is a slow-growing bacterium that primarily affects the lungs but can spread to other organs.

Why is TB special? - It has a very thick, waxy cell wall that makes it resistant to many antibiotics - It grows very slowly — treatment takes months - It can hide inside cells in an inactive (latent) stat

| Pulmonary tuberculosis | Chronic cough >2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats; sputum AFB positive; upper‑lobe infiltrates, cavitation on CXR | Slow progression, constitutional symptoms, positive GeneXpert/AFB; often HIV‑positive |

| Tuberculosis | Weight loss, night sweats, low‑grade fever, persistent cough > 2 weeks, risk factors (HIV, crowded living) | Sputum GeneXpert positive; chest X‑ray shows upper‑lobe infiltrates or cavitation; not primarily mucus‑producing |
Post-infectious (commonest, especially in Kenya): Tuberculosis, severe pneumonia, measles, whooping cough, adenovirus
Silica + TB → silica impairs macrophage killing → facilitates Mycobacterium tuberculosis replication → synergistic increase in TB incidence (silico‑tuberculosis).

Silicosis: Silica (quartz) dust — Miners, quarry and stone workers, sandblasters, tunnellers, ceramics, masons — Upper-zone nodules, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes, progressive massive fibrosis; high risk of TB (silico-tuberculosis), lung cancer, COPD, autoimmune disease

| Pulmonary tuberculosis | Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss; endemic exposure; cavitary lesion in upper lobes | Acid‑fast bacilli on sputum smear / GeneXpert; response to anti‑TB therapy; granulomatous pattern on biopsy, not malignant cells |
In Kenya, pulmonary tuberculosis with mediastinal lymphadenopathy can also cause nerve involvement and must be ruled out with sputum microscopy/culture and possibly GeneXpert.

qs.q: A health district implements a policy where community health volunteers actively search for active tuberculosis cases by visiting households in high-density settlements. This strategy shifts surveillance from passive to:
o: Centralized quarantine restricting local movement.
Tertiary rehabilitative care for chronic lung scarring.
Laboratory research on mycobacterial genetics.
Active community case finding for early detection.
Passive clinic record keeping without outreach.
qs.e: Active case finding involves health workers going into communities to find hidden cases.

qs.q: A laboratory technician is handling a culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Which specific safety precaution is most critical to prevent aerosol transmission from the culture?
o: Working inside a Class II biosafety cabinet
Using a standard open laboratory burner
Wearing standard protective nitrile gloves
Wearing a standard protective surgical mask
Thoroughly disinfecting the laboratory bench
qs.e: A Class II biosafety cabinet provides filtered air protection against aerosolized mycobacteria.

qs.q: A patient with advanced HIV presents with chronic pulmonary disease resembling tuberculosis. Acid-fast staining reveals mycobacteria, but identification shows a non-tuberculous mycobacterium. Which species is most likely?
o: Infecting patients via Mycobacterium avium
Infecting patients via Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Infecting patients via Mycobacterium leprae
Infecting patients via Mycobacterium bovis
Infecting patients via Mycobacterium kansasii
qs.e: Mycobacterium avium complex is a common opportunistic pathogen in AIDS patients with low CD4 counts.

qs.q: A patient with advanced HIV develops a chronic pulmonary illness resembling tuberculosis. Laboratory acid-fast stain is positive, but molecular probes identify a non-tuberculous mycobacterium. Which species is most common?
o: Mycobacterium ulcerans producing the necrotizing toxin
Mycobacterium avium complex causing systemic dissemination
Mycobacterium kansasii presenting with cavitary disease
Mycobacterium fortuitum infecting post-surgical sites
Mycobacterium leprae tropism for peripheral nerves
qs.e: Mycobacterium avium complex is the most frequent non-tuberculous mycobacterial pathogen causing opportunistic infections in advanced AIDS.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the main way Mycobacterium tuberculosis is transmitted between people?
o: Sharing contaminated eating utensils such as forks or spoons
Inhaling airborne droplets generated by coughing or sneezing
Direct physical contact through skin-to-skin exposure
Consuming contaminated food or unpasteurized dairy products
qs.e: TB is spread by inhaling airborne particles containing bacilli. The other listed routes are not typical for TB transmission.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Sputum antimicrobial susceptibility testing for a 14-year-old adolescent with persistent pulmonary tuberculosis demonstrates resistance to several first-line agents. The strain is classified as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Resistance to which pair of medications defines this classification?
o: Isoniazid and ethambutol
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol
Isoniazid and rifampicin
Rifampicin and pyrazinamide
qs.e: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin. Resistance to rifampicin paired with pyrazinamide or ethambutol in the absence of isoniazid resistance does not fulfill the criteria for MDR-TB.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Sputum collected from an 8-year-old child presenting with chronic cough and weight loss undergoes diagnostic microscopy. The cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis contains high concentrations of mycolic acids. Which microscopic staining property is directly imparted by this cell wall lipid content?
o: Retention of crystal violet following Gram decolorization
Retention of carbol fuchsin following acid-alcohol decolorization
Resistance to background dye uptake during negative staining
Selective deposition of silver stain within intracellular structures
qs.e: Mycolic acids render the cell wall hydrophobic and resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol, allowing the organism to retain carbol fuchsin during acid-fast staining. Standard Gram-positive organisms retain crystal violet, whereas mycobacteria stain poorly on conventional Gram stain due to this lipid barrier.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A 15-year-old adolescent who successfully completed a 6-month regimen for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years ago presents with recurrent fever, night sweats, and a new cavitary lung lesion. Sputum culture is positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. How is this patient's treatment history classified?
o: Patient classified as relapse
Patient classified as new case
Patient classified as lost to follow-up
Patient classified as treatment failure
qs.e: A patient previously declared cured or having completed treatment who presents with a recurrent episode of culture-positive tuberculosis is classified as a relapse. Treatment failure is designated when a patient remains culture-positive or becomes positive again at month 5 or later during active therapy.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: MCQs

es.q: List and explain the classification of tuberculosis according to drug susceptibility.
es.m:
- **Drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB):** The organism is susceptible to the medicines in the intended standard regimen.
- **Isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB):** Resistance to isoniazid, with susceptibility to rifampicin.
- **Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB):** Resistance to rifampicin, with or without resistance to other medicines.
- **Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB):** Resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin.
- **Pre-XDR-TB:** MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to any fluoroquinolone.
- **XDR-TB:** MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance and additional resistance to at least one key Group A medicine (bedaquiline or linezolid).
es.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: Essay questions

es.q: Outline the pathophysiology and immunology of tuberculosis from inhalation to granuloma formation.
es.m:
- **Inhalation:** Infectious droplet nuclei reach the alveoli.
- **Phagocytosis:** Alveolar macrophages engulf the bacilli, which can inhibit normal intracellular killing and survive within macrophages.
- **Early multiplication:** Bacilli multiply locally and may spread through lymphatics to hilar lymph nodes and via the bloodstream.
- **Cell-mediated immunity:** T lymphocytes, particularly Th1 cells, produce interferon-gamma which activates macrophages, while tumour necrosis factor-alpha helps maintain granuloma structure.
- **Granuloma formation:** Epithelioid macrophages and Langhans-type giant cells surround a central area that may undergo caseous necrosis.

es.q: Describe the clinical features and presentations of extrapulmonary tuberculosis at common anatomical sites.
es.m:
- **Lymph node:** Chronic, often painless enlarged nodes that may become matted or form a sinus.
- **Pleural:** Fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough and breathlessness.
- **Meningeal:** Persistent headache, fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, seizures or cranial nerve palsies.
- **Spinal/bone:** Chronic back pain, spinal tenderness, deformity, abscess or neurological deficit.
- **Abdominal & Genitourinary:** Abdominal pain, distension, ascites, fever, weight loss, altered bowel habit, or sterile pyuria, haematuria, flank pain and infertility.

es.q: List the key risk factors that increase the risk of progression from tuberculosis infection to active disease.
es.m:
- **HIV infection:** Especially with a low CD4 count.
- **Exposure:** Close household exposure to infectious pulmonary TB.
- **Age:** Age below 5 years, especially infants, who are more likely to develop severe disseminated TB and TB meningitis.
- **Nutritional and metabolic state:** Undernutrition, low body weight, and diabetes mellitus.
- **Medical conditions and therapy:** Silicosis, chronic kidney disease, some malignancies, and immunosuppressive therapy (tumour necrosis factor inhibitors and prolonged systemic corticosteroids).
- **Lifestyle and history:** Smoking, harmful alcohol use, overcrowding, poor ventilation, and previous TB treatment or drug-resistant TB exposure.
es.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: Essay questions

ai.clinicalScope: Active pulmonary tuberculosis in adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Tuberculosis is a contagious lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It spreads through tiny droplets when an infected person coughs, and it is a leading cause of death worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic granulomatous disease of the lung caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted by airborne droplets.
b: WHO estimates ~10 million new cases annually; > 80 % occur in low‑ and middle‑income countries.
In East Africa, TB incidence is 200–300 per 100 000 population.
HIV co‑infection triples the risk of progression from latent to active disease.
Most cases are pulmonary; extrapulmonary disease accounts for ~15 %.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Active disease follows inhalation of bacilli and failure of host immunity.
b: Close contact with an untreated smear‑positive case.
HIV infection (CD4 < 200 cells/µL).
Diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, alcoholism, smoking.
Silica exposure (miners, quarry workers) – silico‑tuberculosis.
Use of immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., steroids, anti‑TNF).

sections.p: After inhalation, bacilli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but survive within phagosomes due to a waxy cell wall.
b: Delayed‑type hypersensitivity (type IV) leads to granuloma formation.
Caseating necrosis creates cavitation, especially in upper lobes where oxygen tension is high.
Latent infection persists in granulomas; reactivation occurs when immunity wanes.
HIV impairs CD4‑mediated macrophage activation, accelerating progression.

sections.p: Symptoms develop insidiously over weeks to months.
b: Persistent cough ≥2 weeks, often productive of scant sputum.
Low‑grade fever, night sweats, weight loss (cachexia).
Hemoptysis (usually small) from cavity erosion.
Chest pain pleuritic if pleural involvement.
In HIV‑positive patients, presentation may be atypical or extrapulmonary.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical guide the need for microbiology and imaging.
b: Ask about cough duration, sputum characteristics, fever pattern, weight change, night sweats, and exposure to known TB cases.
Screen for HIV, diabetes, smoking, occupational silica.
Inspect for cachexia, clubbing, and chest wall deformities.
Auscultation: crackles over upper zones, possible pleural rub.
Percussion: dullness over cavitary area; shifting dullness suggests pleural effusion.

sections.p: Consider other diseases that cause chronic cough and weight loss.
b: Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection (e.g., M. avium complex).
Chronic bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Klebsiella).
Lung cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma.
Silicosis with secondary infection.
Fungal infections (e.g., histoplasmosis).

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise algorithm that works even when some tests are unavailable.

t.b: Detects acid‑fast bacilli; ≥1 + in 2 of 3 samples confirms active TB.
Detects DNA of M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance; positive result = TB, resistance guides regimen.
Shows upper‑lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or miliary pattern; helps assess severity.
Identifies co‑infection; positive result mandates ART integration.
Anemia common; leukocytosis may suggest superinfection.

t.a: If GeneXpert unavailable: sputum culture on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium
t.b: Gold standard but takes 4–8 weeks; positive culture confirms TB.

sections.p: WHO classifies pulmonary TB as ‘new’, ‘relapse’, ‘treatment after failure’, or ‘treatment after loss to follow‑up’. Clinical severity is gauged by symptom burden and radiographic extent.
b: Mild: limited infiltrates, no cavitation, weight loss <10 %.
Moderate: cavitation, weight loss 10–20 %, hemoptysis.
Severe: extensive bilateral disease, massive hemoptysis, respiratory failure.
Miliary or disseminated disease counts as severe regardless of chest findings.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local resource limits affect diagnosis and outcome.
b: HIV may produce atypical radiographs (e.g., lower‑lobe infiltrates).
Diabetes predisposes to treatment failure and relapse.
Concurrent bacterial pneumonia can mask TB signs.
Limited laboratory capacity may force reliance on clinical scoring.

sections.p: Standardised short‑course therapy (6 months) is recommended; modify only for drug resistance or intolerance.
b: Intensive phase (2 months): isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (HRZE).
Continuation phase (4 months): isoniazid + rifampicin (HR).
Directly observed therapy (DOT) ensures adherence in low‑resource settings.
Monitor liver function, visual acuity (ethambutol), and sputum conversion at 2 months.
If rifampicin resistance detected, switch to second‑line regimen per national guidelines.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications reduces mortality.
b: Hemoptysis >100 mL/24 h → urgent bronchoscopy or embolisation.
Pleural effusion with respiratory compromise → thoracentesis.
Miliary TB → start therapy immediately; consider adjunctive steroids if CNS involvement.
Drug‑induced hepatotoxicity (ALT/AST >3× ULN with symptoms) → pause hepatotoxic drugs.
Treatment failure (positive sputum at 5 months) → assess adherence, resistance.
Pregnant women: avoid streptomycin; HRZE is safe.
Children <5 years: higher risk of disseminated disease; use weight‑based dosing.
Elderly: monitor for drug toxicity, comorbidities.
HIV‑positive: start ART 2 weeks after TB therapy, unless CD4 < 50 cells/µL (then start within 2 weeks).

sections.p: With proper treatment, cure rates exceed 85 % even in low‑resource settings.
b: Sputum smear conversion by 2 months predicts good outcome.
Schedule follow‑up visits at 2, 5, and 6 months to assess adherence and side effects.
BCG vaccination at birth provides partial protection against severe pediatric TB.
Infection control: cough etiquette, ventilation, and isolation of smear‑positive patients.
Contact tracing and prophylactic isoniazid for children <5 years.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Smear microscopy may be negative in early disease or HIV; rely on GeneXpert or culture.
Chest X‑ray can be normal in HIV patients despite active TB.
Elevated ESR is non‑specific; use in conjunction with clinical picture.
Rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert requires confirmatory line‑probe assay before changing regimen.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent fever despite 2 months of therapy

faq.q: Why is GeneXpert preferred over smear microscopy?
faq.a: It detects TB DNA rapidly and identifies rifampicin resistance, improving early appropriate therapy.

faq.q: Can TB be cured without DOT?
faq.a: Cure rates drop markedly without supervised therapy because of poor adherence and resistance development.

faq.q: Is a normal chest X‑ray enough to rule out TB?
faq.a: No; especially in HIV patients, TB can be radiographically occult, so microbiology is essential.

exam: What is the next best step after a patient with a 3‑week cough and weight loss has a negative sputum smear but high clinical suspicion? — Obtain GeneXpert or send sputum for culture; consider chest X‑ray.
How does HIV infection alter the radiographic appearance of pulmonary TB? — It often produces lower‑lobe infiltrates, less cavitation, and may be normal.

Explain why rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert mandates a change in regimen. — Rifampicin is a cornerstone of the 6‑month regimen; resistance predicts multidrug‑resistant TB requiring second‑line drugs.
A patient on HRZE develops jaundice and ALT 250 U/L. What should you do? — Stop all hepatotoxic drugs, assess for other causes, and restart with a modified regimen once liver enzymes improve.
Which clinical feature most strongly predicts cavitary disease? — Persistent cough with hemoptysis and weight loss >10 %.

Describe the infection‑control measures needed in a crowded ward with a smear‑positive TB patient. — Place patient in a well‑ventilated area or isolation, use surgical masks for staff and visitors, encourage cough etiquette.
Why is DOT especially important in low‑resource settings? — It overcomes barriers to adherence such as cost, travel, and health‑system gaps, reducing resistance.
What is the rationale for giving ethambutol in the intensive phase? — It prevents emergence of resistance while awaiting susceptibility results.

How would you differentiate pulmonary TB from non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection on sputum testing? — GeneXpert is specific for M. tuberculosis; culture with species identification differentiates NTM.

A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive man on ART presents with fever, cough, and a chest X‑ray showing diffuse micronodules. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Miliary TB; start full anti‑TB regimen promptly and consider adjunctive steroids if CNS involvement is suspected.
